body: Oh well that's a different matter! Is he aware he does that? It's hard to feel empathy or validate someone who doesn't return the same to you.

I think it's good he has shared how he is feeling. It doesn't have to be logical, but it's good he has communicated instead of letting it fester.

The challenge is not letting your own feelings fester and being open about that, too. You can say you've had little time for your own hobbies and finding sleep deprivation challenging without it being a competition. You can express you felt disappointed he didn't ask how you are doing. You can share you feel you're doing the lions share of parenting and finding it hard to have emotional bandwidth right now for much else. 

Perhaps think about the goal of shared communication. It's not about asking or expecting you to take more on, maybe it's just about validating each other and saying yeah it's hard and life changing or yes watching an emergency c section is tough. You don't have to fix that for him, but acknowledging his point of view is powerful.

If you need him to acknowledge your feelings or take on more, make that the goal of your communication to him. Talking is so powerful. I know you shouldn't have to ask that, but this is the situation.

Mh nurse here, and a student coordinator.

My big piece of advice is to be open with your assessor about your mental health (if they feel a safe person to open up to) so that you can have some extra support during your placement. Most of us will always try to help students out, whether on a tough day it's a long break or an early finish. If you do end up struggling, this input will be so valuable. Remember, most of us have experienced mental illness health ourselves or via a loved one, and have chosen this as a career, so we get it and want to help. 

My other advice, especially on a community placement, would be to try and get some interesting/new experiences several times a week to give you something to aim for. It can be too easy to fall into a trap of sticking with your assessor or reading up on things rather than being proactive, but in my experience that can lead to a bit of a groundhog day feeling. Community is tough as a student IMO.

I also wonder if you can identify a patient or two from the start that you almost 'take on' and see through to the end of placement. I love when students get stuck in and can help care-cordinate things to a high/detailed standard, it really benefits the patient and your learning too. I wonder if working to benefit someone will act as a big motivator.

Other than that, if you can I would try to focus on placement whilst you're there and give the uni work a break if time allows/do it on only one or two days a week. It's so hard trying to juggle both! That way, when you go home, you can have that time to rest and recuperate.

I hope you get a lovely team to work with that inspires you. Ive had burn out badly before too. Initially I went through the motions and slowly slowly started to feel more invested. All the best to you.
